Subject: Post-call recap: SLA translations & token-bucket mapping

Hi Maya / QuickShip team,

Thanks for the 30-minute sync this morning — useful conversation. High-level recap and the small set of asks so we can convert the call into an actionable sizing + SLO plan: 

Summary of what you shared (please correct if I got anything wrong):
- Peak crest: short bursts (~30–90s) when arrivals spike from campaigns — crest observed about 5–7x/day.
- Peak magnitude (crest): ~350 QPS for the inference endpoint, average payload ~24 tokens per request (est. crest token-rate ~8.4k tokens/sec).
- Basal (steady) load: ~18–22 QPS outside crest windows (~430–530 tokens/sec).
- Typical response shape: majority of requests are short generations (<=200 tokens); occasional long-turn summaries up to ~2,000 tokens.
- Streaming: ~12% of flows use streaming (multi-turn assistant-style); streaming turns average ~80 tokens/turn.
- Latency target you care about: interactive flows p95 ~400ms, p99 target TBD (you mentioned wanting <1s ideally for non-streaming short answers).

Immediate asks / next deliveries:
1) We will map the crest->basal translation to a sizing sketch (QPS, tokens/sec, concurrency) and show model placement + fallback recommendations.
2) Diego will follow up with a short list of technical clarifying questions (stream semantics, retry policy, client-side concurrency).
3) Please upload the sample traffic CSV we requested (one-week sample, anonymized) — I attached a template (qs_traffic_sample.csv) and a suggested SLO matrix (qs_slo_matrix.xlsx) for you to fill.

Target timeframe: we’ll aim to deliver the initial sizing sketch and SLO mapping by EOW (Fri, Nov 6). If you can get the sample traffic before EOD Thu that helps tighten the numbers.

Thanks — and happy to hop back on a quick 20-min engineering workshop if you prefer we walk through the numbers live.

Best,
Marissa
Marissa Cole
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: SLA translations & token-bucket mapping

Thanks for the recap, Marissa — a couple of technical clarifications that will materially change the sizing: 

1) Streaming semantics: when you say "streaming" are we talking about long-lived gRPC/websocket streams where multiple turns share a single connection (server pushes partial tokens), or are these short-lived chunked responses per-turn? If long-lived, what is the max concurrent open streams we should assume (not turns)?

2) Concurrency per user: do clients open multiple simultaneous requests per user (e.g., background checks + interactive), or is concurrency ~1 request per active user? For rough capacity math, concurrency multiplies effective QPS.

3) Long-turns distribution: you mentioned occasional 2k-token summaries — can you say how frequent those are (e.g., 0.1% of requests, 1% of requests)? That affects memory/KV cache sizing and kernel selection.

4) Retry/backoff policy: are clients configured to retry immediately on 5xx or to backoff? Short aggressive retries can create crest amplification.

Sizing note / quick back-of-envelope: taking your crest estimate (350 QPS) with 24 tokens/request gives ~8.4k tokens/sec aggregate. At 8k tokens/sec sustained across several seconds, model choice + batching profile matters: a 70B quantized variant might be 2–3x more expensive than a smaller 13B optimized for streaming. We should model both options and show cost/latency tradeoffs.

If you can paste a 2–4 hour CSV snippet into the Drive link Marissa mentioned (or reply-all with it), I’ll run a quick script to produce the crest-duration histogram and a token-by-second chart.

—Diego
Diego Fernandez
Principal Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa and Diego — great summary. Quick answers inline: 

- Streaming: those are short-lived chunked streams per turn (client opens per-turn, not long-lived multi-turn streams). So assume one stream per turn; peak concurrent streams ~= peak concurrent requests.
- Concurrency per user: ~1 (clients are single-tab web UI). Occasionally our monitoring pipelines peek concurrently but that’s <5% of traffic.
- Long turns: ~0.4% of requests exceed 1,000 tokens; ~0.05% exceed 1,500 tokens. Most requests are 20–80 tokens.
- Retry policy: client retries with exponential backoff; most retries are after 500ms, which mitigates immediate crest amplification.

To confirm numbers from above: crest bursts are typically 30–60s and hit ~320–360 QPS at the peak; basal 18–22 QPS. I uploaded a 6-hour sample and a short dashboard link here: https://drive.google.com/qs-traffic-sample (anonymized).

SLO targets: interactive chat (streaming chunks) — p95 <= 400ms, p99 <= 850ms for per-chunk delivery. Non-streamed short generations: p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms. For long-turn outputs (>=1k tokens) we accept higher tail latencies but need progress updates (streaming preferred).

Hope that helps — let us know if you want different slices from the traffic dump.

—Maya
Maya Patel
Head of Platform Engineering, QuickShip Logistics

2) Marissa: confirm business-critical flows (chat vs. batch summarization) and which flows must hit the p99 targets. Add to the SLO sheet. Due: Thu EOD.
3) Me (Karthik): prepare 1-page sizing sketch with two deployment variants: (A) low-latency path (smaller optimized model + more replicas, preferred for interactive chat), (B) cost-efficient path (larger quantized model with batched execution), including fallback policy and expected per-10k-token cost delta. Draft due: Fri EOD.
